newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Finland fancied for early EMU membership.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Finland fancied for early EMU membership.

text.p: Finland, already a strong front-runner for founder membership of a single European currency, looks set to meet all of the economic targets for monetary union, a Reuters survey showed on Wednesday.

In a Europe-wide poll of economists on how countries are shaping up to meet the Maastricht criteria for membership of economic and monetary union (EMU), Finland was one of only two countries which, according to the average findings, would get a clean bill of health.
The median of 24 forecasts submitted on the Finnish economy showed that Helsinki's inflation, debt, budget deficit and interest rate levels would all meet the Maastricht targets.
In previous quarterly polls, Luxembourg alone had been forecast to meet all of the economic criteria.

Average predictions for Finland's 1997 debt burden were seen in earlier surveys to overshoot the Maastricht guidelines, but this time its average debt to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio was given as 60 percent, which meets the European Union target.
"Expenditure cuts implemented this year with good GDP growth are the main reasons for the expected improvement in total debt," said Juha Ahtola, chief economist at Merita Bank Finland.
A separate monthly poll on the likelihood of EMU starting on time showed 44 out of 49 contributors thought Finland would be a founder member of the euro club.

Finland was given on average a 90 percent chance of joining from the start, while those taking part in the survey who predicted a delay put the average lag before the markka would join the single currency club at two years.

"There is still some opposition to Finnish entry to EMU, but it is not great. I think compared with other countries we are eager to go in," said Paavo Suni of ETLA, the Research Institute of the Finnish Economy.
"The general feeling is that it would be better to be in than out -- to stay outside you would have very few options."

Bullish sentiments for Finland's early EMU entry were further boosted this week by European Union finance ministers, who on Monday agreed to drop Finland from a list of countries which were feared to be running excessive budget deficits.
